#4606. Toyota’s EV sales more than doubled in a year, but gas cars are getting crushed in China

Toyota’s EV sales have jumped 127% through September, but that isn’t telling the whole story. Slumping demand for gas and hybrid cars in China has pushed global sales lower for three months in a row.

Including Lexus, Toyota sold 309,766 battery electric vehicles (BEVs) globally through the first nine months of 2026, up 127.4% from the same period last year.

Except for January (+87.5%), Toyota’s EV sales have more than doubled every month this year compared with 2025.

The higher demand comes after Toyota and Lexus launched updated versions of their first-gen electric SUVs, the bZ4X (now the bZ in the US) and the RZ.

Toyota has added several new electric models, including the C-HR+ (C-HR in the US), bZ4X Touring (bZ Woodland in the US), and Urban Cruiser, while Lexus now offers the ES EV. Both brands will introduce a three-row electric SUV, which is expected to go on sale over the next few months.

According to data from Cleantechnica, the Toyota bZ4X became the 20th best-selling EV worldwide through August, with nearly 100,000 units sold.

While its EVs are catching on, Toyota Motor’s global sales fell for the third straight month in September.

Toyota sold 860,107 vehicles in September, down 2.2% from the previous year. The company said that although overall demand remained steady, sales in China fell, leading to lower overall sales than last year.

Through September, Toyota sold 7.51 million vehicles globally, down 3.4%. In China, Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20%, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales.

Toyota said the overall market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” resulting in lower sales.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Toyota sells several electric vehicles through its two joint ventures (GAC Toyota and FAW Toyota) in China, including the bZ3, bZ3X, bZ5, and bZ7.

After the US, China is Toyota’s second-largest market. Through September, Toyota has now sold more vehicles in its home market of Japan (1.19 million) than in China.

To turn things around and compete with companies like BYD, Toyota, like many major OEMs nowadays, is increasingly adopting more Chinese EV tech and manufacturing practices.

Nikkei reported in August that Toyota plans to build a new Lexus electric SUV in China, rather than in Japan as it has traditionally. Production is expected to begin at Lexus’ new manufacturing plant in Shanghai next fall.

Toyota's EV sales still represent less than 3% of its overall sales. This is the real news.

BTW, Toyota's European sales got hit in a similar way. They are up 0,7% YoY but that's compared to a rising overall market of 5,7%. This lead to it's market share shrinking.

The new Lexus EV will use advanced manufacturing methods, including gigacasting, to cut costs and speed up production.

Toyota isn’t the only legacy automaker struggling to keep pace in China’s fast-moving automotive market.

Volkswagen Group CFO and COO, Arno Antilitz, admitted the company “must act quickly and decisively” after reporting third-quarter sales in China dropped 38% to 405,800 units on Thursday. The company also plans to use technology developed in China for its next-gen EVs, which it will sell overseas.

#4605. Send your name to Saturn’s largest moon

Published Oct 30, 2026 2:34 PM EDT

NASA is still on track to send its Dragonfly rotocraft to Saturn’s moon Titan by the end of the decade, and you can come along for the ride. Well, you can at least add your initials to the flight roster.

As part of its Journey to Titan campaign, NASA has opened an online registry that will be included on a microchip aboard the spacecraft when it launches. The launch is currently scheduled for no earlier than July 2028. Signees will receive a personalized digital “boarding pass,” as proof that their names will reach the ice-encased Saturnian moon in 2034. While the encoded autographs may not do much to help with the overall mission, it’s nice to know that you will be represented on what may become one of the most consequential space endeavors of all time.

“We are excited to bring humanity along for the journey of a lifetime, and we invite everyone to send their names on this small, but mighty rotorcraft that will unlock the secrets of the universe,” Nicky Fox, NASA’s Science Mission Directorate associate administrator, said in the announcement.

Titan is the largest of Saturn’s 292 known moons, and a longtime dream destination in the search for life beyond Earth. Although Titan features dusty dunes overlooking lakes and rivers of methane, the frigid surface also maintains a temperature of around −290 degrees Fahrenheit. This is inhospitable to life as we know it, but a giant ocean also exists beneath the icy shell. Astrobiologists widely agree that these waters probably contain enough complex compounds to facilitate a prebiotic environment. Laboratory simulations of Titan’s atmosphere have also indicated its gaseous conditions can even form some of the principle building blocks for DNA and RNA. If true, extraterrestrial microbial life may exist within the moon’s hidden waters.

However, there’s no way to confirm the possibility without directly examining Titan’s conditions. That’s where Dragonfly comes into play. After over six years of interplanetary travel, NASA’s eight-bladed robotic rotocraft will land on the moon and begin its environmental survey. Dragonfly’s vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) capabilities will allow it to travel to multiple locations over the planned three-year mission. If all goes well, the rotocraft will journey across 70 miles on Titan, while visiting 20 to 30 different areas.

“By flying the first-ever rotorcraft science mission, NASA will…we search for signs of habitability on a distant world that is most similar to our own,” added Fox.

Dragonfly is currently under construction at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland. It marks the fourth mission in NASA’s New Frontiers Program, which is dedicated to further exploration of the planets and moons that comprise our solar system.

Adding your name to Dragonfly’s log is likely a no-brainer for many people, but there is no rush if you need to take some time to ponder the decision. Signees have until 11:59 p.m. EST on January 15, 2027, to make their (digital) mark.

#4603. Rivian’s electric van gets 30% more range and AWD, now delivering

Rivian has started delivering the first major hardware upgrade to its electric van since production began in 2021: a bigger LFP battery pack good for 30% more range, and a new dual-motor AWD version.

The company confirmed in its Q3 2026 shareholder presentation that deliveries of the new variants began in early October. That’s the first real spec bump for a van that has been stuck at about 160 miles of rated range for years.

Rivian first mentioned the upgrade in its Q4 2025 letter, which we covered in February when Amazon’s fleet of Rivian vans grew 50%. At the time, Rivian only said it was “developing” a larger battery and AWD to “expand EDV route coverage” in Amazon’s network.

Now it’s shipping. In today’s presentation, Rivian says the new variants are “specifically designed to expand route coverage into more rural networks,” with the AWD configuration and the bigger pack offering “a 30% increase in range.”

EPA certification documents for the 2027 EDV 700, issued September 17, list the new pack at 129 kWh usable. Rivian has marketed the current van with a 100 kWh LFP pack, so that’s roughly 29% more energy, which lines up with the 30% range claim.

The upgrade is limited to the bigger 700 van, the one with 652 cubic feet of cargo space. The smaller 500 keeps its existing pack and front-wheel drive.

The EPA filing gives unadjusted lab range figures, which always run high because they skip the correction for real-world driving:

Rivian rates the current 700 at “up to 160 miles.” Apply Rivian’s 30% to that and the new FWD van lands around 208 miles. Using the AWD van’s smaller 23% gain from the EPA tests, we estimate the dual-motor version at about 195 to 200 miles.

So AWD costs roughly a third of the range gain. For a van, that’s a fine trade. Rural routes mean longer distances between stops, plus gravel, mud, and snow, which is exactly where a front-wheel-drive van with a full load of packages in the back struggles.

200 miles is roughly what Rivian promised for the van when deliveries to Amazon started in 2022, before the rated figure settled closer to 160 miles. Rivian is finally there, four years later.

The timing helps on the sales side too. Rivian’s van business is still overwhelmingly Amazon, years after the exclusivity period ended in late 2023. We spotted a Rivian van in Walmart+ livery on a car hauler in Indiana just this week, though neither company has announced a deal.

The competition has also thinned out. GM ended BrightDrop van production in Ontario and Canoo went bankrupt, leaving Ford’s E-Transit as the main full-size electric alternative in the US.

Rivian needs to make the sales to USPS. I am starting to see those vans all the time now. It looks like it is designed from ground up to optimize for delivery. Extra height for drivers, lower floor of entry, great visibility in the front. Low bumper and lower headlight position for safety. Overall, great design.

Too bad that GM dropped Brightdrop van just as they are getting popular. I see a lot of FedEx trucks are now Bright drop. Perfect timing when diesel price is thru the roof. GM never have the long term view and always good at starting something but give up just before it becomes a hot seller.

This is the upgrade the van needed. 160 miles was always fine for dense urban Amazon routes, but it boxed Rivian out of a big chunk of the fleet market: rural delivery, utilities, telecom, anyone who can’t guarantee a short loop and an overnight charge.

Getting to around 200 miles real-world, with AWD as an option, opens a lot of those routes. And unlike most of the EV van market right now, Rivian is actually building and improving its product rather than killing it.

The question is whether Rivian can turn that into customers other than Amazon. A Walmart+ wrap on a car hauler is a nice sign. We’d want to see a real order. If you’re running a fleet and these specs change your math, we’d love to hear from you.

#4602. Psychedelic nasal spray treats depression with toad-inspired goo

Published Oct 30, 2026 3:45 PM EDT

A powerful psychedelic compound best associated with the Sonoran desert toad (Incilius alvarius) has been recreated in a lab and transformed into a fast-acting nasal spray. A recent clinical trial outlined this week in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) suggests this spray could help people with treatment resistant depression, without the often less pleasant element of psychedelics. In the study, a single squeeze of the spray eased patients’ depressive symptoms with benefits lasting throughout the eight week trial.

Crucially, those long-term benefits (which have also been observed in other psychedelic research) didn’t require enduring an all-day mystical trip. Most patients were cleared for release less than two hours after taking the spray. Thankfully, the approach also eliminates the need to fondle a toxic amphibian. That’s potentially a plus both for patients and overharvested toad populations. The finds come amid a resurgence in new research and investment involving psychedelics, supported in part by evolving political attitudes towards the compounds on federal and state levels.

The nasal spray was developed by biotech firm AtaiBeckley. Its  active ingredient is called mebufotenin, which is also known as 5-MeO-DMT. The compound occurs naturally in several places, but it is most famously associated with the secretions of the Sonoran desert toad. For decades, amateur psychonauts have sought out these meaty North American toads for the prominent glands located on the amphibian’s head and hind legs. Squeezing those glands releases a milky secretion (sometimes inaccuracy referred to as venom), which when dried and then vaporized, produces an intense psychedelic experience. Many people who have smoked it describe a profound sense of oneness or ego dissolution, and some even report the sensation of dying.

Though based on the same compound, the drug in the nasal spray is synthetic and made in a lab. The researchers wanted to see if a controlled, clinical dose of 5-MeO-DMT could deliver some of the compound’s reported therapeutic benefits while keeping the overall treatment brief, especially compared with longer-acting psychedelics like psilocybin. They  limited their study to 193 adults between the ages of 18 to 75 with treatment-resistant depression. The participants, who came from the United States, Europe, and Australia, had each already tried at least two antidepressant treatments without success. By some estimates, around a third of all patients experiencing major depressive disorder also have treatment resistant depression.

Each participant received nasal spray in either a low (.3mg), medium (8mg), or high (12mg) dose. Neither the patient, nor the clinical staff or researchers involved knew which dose was given. The most intense psychedelic effects wore off relatively quickly, regardless of the dose. Clinicians checked on the patients at regular intervals to determine if they were deemed safe enough to leave the clinic. Among participants who received the 8-milligram dose, 85 percent were ready for discharge within two hours, compared with 78 percent of those who received the 12-milligram dose.

However, the therapeutic effects of the spray appeared to persist far longer.  Patients who received the medium or high dose showed significantly greater improvement than the comparison group as early as two days after treatment, and that advantage held through the end of the eight-week study. The team measured depression with a clinical scale measuring from 0 to 60, with  higher scores indicating more severe symptoms. After four weeks, the 12 mg group had dropped an average of 11.1 points on that score. The 8mg group dropped an even higher 12.5 points while the .3mg group dropped 5.5 points. These findings suggest the nasal spray application could provide some of the same therapeutic effects of other scheduled therapies less less need to have healthcare workers monitoring patients for many hours at a time.

“In adults with treatment-resistant depression, single doses of intranasal mebufotenin benzoate were well tolerated and produced rapid, robust, and durable reductions in depressive symptoms,” the study authors write. “Intranasal mebufotenin benzoate may improve treatment access and convenience, requiring a shorter monitoring period and fewer clinic visits compared with psilocybin and esketamine, respectively.”

This experimental nasal spray arrives amid a transitionary period for psychedelic research. State governments have shown more interest in the field in recent years, with Oregon and Colorado each launching their own psilocybin programs. Even Texas, a state traditionally associated with a tough on drugs approach, just committed $50 million to research the powerful psychedelic ibogaine. Signs of movement are occurring at the federal level as well. In April, President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at accelerating research and FDA approval of psychedelic-based therapies.

Though it attracted significant attention, the executive order is really more signaling than action. It notably does not lower the bar a therapeutic needs to reach before archived FDA approval.

Still, pharmaceutical companies are clearly taking note. Earlier this year, Eli Lilly, the largest pharmaceutical company in the world, acquired AtariBeckley for $2.8 billion. AtaiBeckley developed the nasal spray used in the recent JAMA study.

#4598. Someone ran Rivian’s pedal-by-wire e-bike out of battery and things got weird

The ALSO TM-B is one of the most technologically interesting new e-bikes to hit the road in years, largely because it does away with one of the most fundamental parts of a bicycle: the mechanical connection between the pedals and rear wheel. With only copper wires connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, the TM-B is one of the most revolutionary new e-bikes in years.

But that raises an obvious question. What happens when the battery dies?

One early Launch Edition owner, Aaron Draczynski, decided to find out by deliberately running his TM-B down toward empty to see whether ALSO’s drive-by-wire system would leave him stranded.

He shared the experience on YouTube, discovering that the answer is surprisingly complicated – and involves something called “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Unlike a conventional e-bike, where the rider’s pedaling mechanically turns the rear wheel through a chain or belt, the ALSO TM-B uses a pedal-by-wire drivetrain. Pedaling generates electricity, while the rear wheel is driven electrically.

That arrangement enables all sorts of interesting features, including electronically simulated gearing and the Launch Edition’s massive Level 10 boost mode, which can multiply rider input by up to 10 times.

But it also means there’s no traditional drivetrain to fall back on when the battery runs out.

Fortunately, the bike doesn’t simply go from full power to dead.

The owner began his experiment at 31% charge and quickly watched the bike progressively restrict its maximum assist as the battery drained closer to empty. From 23% to 13%, the maximum boost dropped from Level 8 to Level 5 as it began conserving battery.

By 10% charge, the bike was limited to Level 4. At 8%, it dropped to Level 3, followed by Level 2 at 5%. Shortly afterward, only Level 1 remained. Then at 4% battery, conventional electric assistance disappeared entirely.

Interestingly, the normal electronic shifting of the bike’s simulated software gears continued to work through most of that process. But when the battery reached 4%, things changed as the bike started exhibiting issues. The first sign of trouble came when the bike began seemingly randomly shifting gears while in manual mode without the rider even touching the shifter. Several times per second, the bike seemed to want to shift itself between gears.

Keep in mind that the TM-B doesn’t have actual physical gears (and no chain or derailleur, for that matter), but instead simulates various gears using predefined software to make the rider feel like they are working more or less intensely to pedal the bike.

Once the TM-B reached its final low-battery state, an infinity symbol appeared on the display and the bike entered what the owner referred to as “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Instead of using stored battery energy to provide meaningful assistance, the system effectively attempts to pass the rider’s pedaling energy through the electronic drivetrain to keep the rear wheel turning. It’s similar in concept to those old crank-powered flashlights, which, even with a dead storage battery, would still illuminate for as long as the owner cranked them.

And on flat ground, the owner reported that the infinite turtle mode apparently worked surprisingly well.

Draczynski described the experience as roughly equivalent to pedaling a normal bicycle in fourth gear. There was resistance at the pedals, and he could maintain a reasonable pace without feeling like he was simply spinning his legs uselessly.

Then he reached a hill and found the limitation of that effectiveness. Even a slight incline transformed the experience, with the bike feeling more like it was permanently stuck in seventh or eighth gear. Getting home through his hilly neighborhood became, in his words, a “truly grueling ordeal.”

Manual shifting was also disabled in this mode, meaning there was no way to electronically select an easier virtual gear for climbing, since again, there aren’t any physical gears in the bike. Everything in the pedaling experience is software-simulated.

That’s an important limitation for a bike relying entirely on a drive-by-wire drivetrain. The infinite turtle mode might keep you moving with significant effort on level terrain, but it doesn’t turn a dead TM-B into a conventional bicycle, unless that conventional bicycle is being ridden through beach sand.

The low-power state apparently shuts down some other features as well. The owner could no longer lock or unlock the TM-B through ALSO’s smartphone app, though he did report the bike’s touchscreen controls continued working, and he guessed that the bike had shut down connectivity to conserve power for its key systems to operate.

Perhaps more concerning than the low-battery riding experience was what happened when this particular TM-B was simply sitting in the owner’s garage.

Describing another scenario he encountered, Draczynski says he left the bike sitting unplugged in his garage at around 70% charge. The following evening, it had fallen to 40%, and a day later it was down to 18%.

When he returned the next morning, the TM-B displayed a “Bike issue detected” message followed by “Install battery to ride.”

There was just one problem: the battery was already installed.

Plugging in the charger didn’t initially help because the bike apparently couldn’t detect its own battery, and thus charging didn’t begin. Worse, the battery refused to eject using the normal ejection process, leaving the owner unable to remove it and charge it off of the bike.

Ultimately, Draczynski used the physical reset button underneath the frame, which brought the system back to life. The bike recognized the battery again and began charging normally.

Much like modern EVs, I would imagine a lot of these issues will be fixed via a software update. Early adoption is fun but you’re basically beta testing a product for the company at full price.

That degree of overnight battery drain obviously isn’t something we’d expect from a normal e-bike, so hopefully this was either an isolated software issue or something ALSO can address with an update. For his part, Draczynski suspects that the bike might be draining its battery so heavily at rest due to the lack of a cell signal in his garage. “I was quite surprised at the drop from day to day,” he explained on Reddit. “If I had to wager a guess, the bike might be searching for a cellular signal, but there’s no reception in my garage so it’s just draining the battery.”

But the experiment offers an interesting first real-world look at one of the biggest questions surrounding ALSO’s unusual drivetrain.

A normal e-bike with a dead battery becomes a heavy bicycle. The TM-B instead becomes something much stranger: an electricity-generating exercise machine that uses your legs to generate current, electronically sends that current through the bike, and then uses it to turn the rear wheel.

And based on this testing, it does in fact work. Just try not to be at the bottom of a hill when you find out for yourself.

#4596. Harley-Davidson’s electric motorcycle brand LiveWire warns it may not survive

Harley-Davidson-born electric motorcycle maker LiveWire has issued a troubling warning about its financial future, announcing that it has substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating as a going concern. The news sent LiveWire’s stock plunging more than 40% on Thursday morning as the company withdrew its full-year financial guidance.

The announcement comes despite some signs of improving sales, with LiveWire reporting a 38% increase in third-quarter revenue to $7.9 million and a 21% rise in motorcycle unit sales. However, the company continues to burn through cash, reporting a net loss of $18.6 million for the quarter.

LiveWire’s cash reserves have also dwindled significantly, falling from $82.8 million at the end of 2025 to just $39.9 million as of September 30, 2026.

The company has now formed a special restructuring committee to explore potential financing arrangements, strategic partnerships, investments, or even a sale. It also withdrew its previous guidance projecting a $70 million to $80 million operating loss for 2026.

The financial warning comes at a particularly pivotal moment for LiveWire, which is preparing to launch its most affordable electric motorcycles yet.

The upcoming LiveWire S4 Honcho series represents a major departure from the company’s existing premium electric motorcycles, offering smaller, lighter, and significantly more affordable models designed to attract a much broader audience of riders with a starting price below US $5,000.

The lower prices could dramatically increase LiveWire’s sales volumes, especially as the company attempts to move beyond the relatively small market for high-dollar electric motorcycles. The Honcho lineup is also expected to help lower the barrier to entry for new riders, with approachable electric motorcycles that eliminate the complexity of clutch and gear shifting.

LiveWire is also preparing to showcase its latest developments at EICMA in Milan next week, where it is expected to display new models and further expand its upcoming electric motorcycle lineup.

Whether those new motorcycles can arrive quickly enough to turn around the company’s financial situation remains to be seen.

This is genuinely sad news to see. If there’s any legacy motorcycle manufacturer that deserves to succeed in the electric motorcycle space, it’s Harley-Davidson.

Make all the jokes you want about old dudes in leather jackets riding around on loud, chrome-covered motorcycles. But the fact is that Harley-Davidson was taking electric motorcycles seriously when most other major motorcycle manufacturers were still pretending they didn’t exist.

Harley-Davidson didn’t just dip its toes into electric motorcycles. It dove in headfirst, developing the original LiveWire electric motorcycle well over a decade ago and eventually bringing a highly acclaimed production bike to market in 2019. That’s right, Harley-Davidson had a legitimately impressive electric motorcycle on the road before COVID was even a thing. Meanwhile, most of its legacy competitors are only now starting to roll out their first serious electric offerings.

Maybe it's news to Electrek, but while Harley was contemplating electric motorcycles, Zero was selling them for over a decade and continues to do so. There are some high end bikes that Livewire just didn't compete with yet cost $30k when it first came out damaging the brand perception. Newer, lower priced models don't help.

There is also competition from run around eScooters that are way cheaper even cheaper than upcoming Honcho.

And that’s what makes this so frustrating. Harley-Davidson did the hard part. It invested early, developed excellent technology, received rave reviews, and proved that electric motorcycles could be thrilling, premium machines. But building great motorcycles and building a profitable electric motorcycle business have turned out to be two very different challenges.

The timing is especially unfortunate because I genuinely believe LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho series could be exactly what the company needs. These smaller, significantly more affordable electric motorcycles could finally open LiveWire up to a younger audience that doesn’t have $15,000 to drop on a flagship motorcycle but still wants something fun, stylish, and electric for $5,000.

In many ways, that audience seems like a much more natural fit for LiveWire’s branding and ethos than the premium motorcycle market it has been chasing for years.

I really hope LiveWire can find what it needs to get through this difficult period. After spending more than a decade helping drag the legacy motorcycle industry kicking and screaming into the electric age, it would be a real shame to see the company stumble just as its most promising chapter might be about to begin.

#4595. Toyota's New ‘Woodland’ SEMA Concepts Prove Even Minivans Deserve to Go Off-Roading

The brand is reimagining its ‘Woodland’ trim level with five concepts that push the soft-road package to new levels, complete with matching liveries.

Toyota already showed us its vision for tackling snow-covered mountains with its Snowhunter concepts. Naturally, the carmaker chose its most rugged trucks and SUVs as the basis for these snow-conquering machines. But what about minivan owners, or people who drive electric crossovers? What happens when they want to venture off-road? Well, Toyota has something for them this year, too: its new Woodland concepts give the RAV4, Grand Highlander, Sienna, bZ EV, and Crown Signia their own off-road treatment.

Built for the 2026 SEMA Show, the five Woodland concepts give some of Toyota's more family-friendly models an off-road makeover. All five vehicles were developed with a common design theme, one established by the company’s CALTY Design Research branch: combining everything that makes these vehicles great for hauling the family, with an extra dose of adventure.

Each vehicle is finished in Horizon Blue paint. Toyota didn't select that color just because it thought it would look pretty; it's a nod to classic Toyota models from the 1960s, including the Stout, Crown, and Corona. Contrasting the lovely blue shade are black accents on the hoods and roofs, giving the vehicles a distinctive two-tone appearance.

But Toyota didn’t just give the vehicles a paint job and call it a day. The five concepts share several off-road upgrades, including suspension lift kits, oversized fender flares, rugged satin-black wheels wrapped in all-terrain tires, and roof racks with crossbars. That might not be enough to conquer the Rubicon Trail, but it certainly makes these family haulers look ready for something more adventurous than the morning school drop-off.

While all of the concepts are interesting, the most surprising might be the Toyota Sienna version, which goes above and beyond the previous Woodland variant. Minivans excel at taking the whole family to grandma's house or helping a friend move across town, but you don't often see one driving off into the woods. Give one some additional ground clearance and all-terrain tires, however, and suddenly it starts looking like a pretty compelling adventure vehicle.

And that's the point Toyota is making with these concepts. We already know the 4Runner can get you almost anywhere. But with a little help, even the more family-focused vehicles in Toyota's lineup might be capable of taking you considerably farther off the beaten path than you'd expect.

#4594. November skygazing: Planetary alignments, a supermoon, comet, and more

Published Oct 31, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

Autumn is here! The air is crisp, the leaves are falling, and the sky is alive. November brings a whole gamut of celestial phenomena for stargazing enthusiasts from a  planetary prom to a meteor shower that can explode occasionally into the most spectacular of sky shows, and  a comet that won’t return for 21 years Let’s get to it!

Mercury is generally difficult to spot. It’s our solar system’s smallest planet and is often lost in the sun’s haze. But in the middle of this month, this speedy boy is flitting in to join the party that Venus, Mars, and Jupiter are throwing all month. The three larger planets will be in alignment for all of November, festooning the morning sky just before  dawn. Venus will be in the southeastern sky, with Mars high in the eastern sky and Jupiter a bit lower, but also towards the east. And Mercury? Look low in the southeast, and it should be visible just before the sun emerges over the horizon.

As the month continues, Mars and Jupiter will edge closer and closer to one another, casting shy glances at one another across the sky like teenagers at a school dance. They’ll finally slide in for a waltz just before sunrise on November 16, where their conjunction in the eastern sky will be chaperoned by the bright star Regulus. Look to the east, but make sure you stop looking once the sun begins to peek its way into the firmament. No planetary conjunction is worth cooking your eyes.

And once the music stops and Mars and Jupiter will slip gracefully away, the fireworks will begin. The Leonids will be visible all month, but their peak is predicted for November 18. At that time, their radiant point—the point from which the meteors appear to emerge—will be right next to the two disengaging dancers in the constellation Leo. This shower usually produces 10 to 15 meteors per hour. However, in 1966 it exploded into one of the most spectacular displays of celestial pyrotechnics ever seen, with thousands of meteors visible every minute. So you never know what you might see!

This month’s full moon is the first of three consecutive supermoons. As per the ever-indispensable Farmer’s Almanac, it will reach peak illumination while below the horizon at 9:50 a.m. EST on November 24. When  actually visible, it’ll appear brightest on the evenings of November 23 and 24. This month’s moon takes its name from the industrious, dam-building rodents of North America, whose long summers of hard work start to pay off in November, when they retreat to their lodges to wait out the winter. Several other Indigenous nations have names that also refer to what animals get up to during the fall: the Tlingit call it the Digging Moon, to the Algonquin it’s the Whitefish Moon, while the Dakota and Lakota call it the Deer Rutting Moon.

The final event of November: a visit from Comet 161P/Hartley–IRAS. The space rock  will reach perihelion—the point at which it’s closest to the sun—on November 27. At that point, its magnitude will be about 12, which means you’ll want a decent telescope to spot it. The International Comet Quarterly suggests at least using a telescope with at least a 7.8 inch (20 centimeter) aperture. If you’ve got such an apparatus, look to the east-northeast, just above the horizon.

Remember that you’ll get the best experience gazing up at the stars if you get away from any sources of light pollution. You should also give your eyes plenty of time adjust to the darkness, and review our stargazing tips before heading out into the night.

#4592. 3 things you might not know about daylight saving time

Published Oct 31, 2026 1:39 PM EDT

Heads up: The clocks are about to change. The evening of Halloween gets an extra hour as the clocks fall back an hour, meaning you can sleep in on Sunday, November 1.

Complaints about daylight savings are as old as daylight savings itself, and pretty much everyone has an opinion about the practice. As with any such topic, there are all kinds of myths and misunderstandings out there.

This one comes up a lot: the idea that farmers are the reason we have daylight savings. In this version of the story, farmers, who work outside and need to align their workdays with the daylight, were the ones who made the argument for the practice.

In truth, farmers were the main group opposed to daylight savings during World War I. According to the Library of Congress: “The agriculture industry fervently opposed the measure because farming schedules are based on sunrise and sunset not the clock.”

After the war there was a bill to repeal daylight savings, which passed through both houses of Congress. President Woodrow Wilson vetoed that bill, and his statement about the veto acknowledged this wouldn’t make farmers happy.

“I realize the very considerable and in some respects very serious inconveniences to which the daylight-saving law subjects the farmers of the country,” he wrote. Wilson sided with the industrial sector. The veto was overridden, leading to a long period where daylight savings was practiced only in certain areas. For example: New York City observed daylight savings, but rural areas in New York State did not (not what you’d expect if farmers broadly supported daylight savings).

None of this is to say that some farmers don’t support daylight savings time today—it’s just that farmers aren’t the reason the practice exists in America. If anything, they tried to stop it.

There are some “facts” repeated so often that hardly anyone questions them, and “Ben Franklin invented daylight savings time” remains one of them. The problem is that it’s not true.

I’d understand if you’re skeptical—I’m a Canadian journalist trying to steal an achievement from one of America’s founding fathers. But you don’t have to take my word on this one—The Franklin Institute, a museum dedicated to Franklin’s legacy, states that “Daylight saving time is one thing that Franklin did not invent.” The United States didn’t even implement daylight savings until 1918, well over a century after Franklin passed away.

So where did the idea that he invented it come from? Probably from a satirical Journal de Paris article Franklin penned back in 1784.

In that piece he jokingly encouraged the residents of Paris to wake up earlier in the morning, in order to spend less money on candles. He also proposed a tax on shutters, rationing of candles, a prohibition of carriages on the streets after sunset, and church bells ringing at the crack of dawn every day. He, it goes without saying, wasn’t being entirely serious.

So where did the idea for daylight savings come from? New Zealand entomologist George Hudson first proposed intentionally shifting the clock in an 1895 talk to the Wellington Philosophical Society, then followed up with a paper in 1898.

This isn’t a myth, exactly, but it is something that rarely comes up in contemporary discussions about daylight savings. Multiple US states have proposed doing away with standard time entirely. Nationally, the Sunshine Protection Act, which passed the House over the summer, would institute the change from sea to shining sea.

Here’s the thing, though: this isn’t the first time. The US tried making daylight savings permanent during the height of the 1970s energy crisis. The problem was that people hated it. What was supposed to be a two-year experiment lasted less than a year because of a massive change in public opinion.

Support for the change started high, as an October 1974 New York Times article lays out: 79 percent of the public favored the idea in December of 1973, but by February of 1974, that dropped to 42 percent—a 37-point swing. A bill to restore standard time in winter passed the House by a 362 to 16 vote.

What caused the backlash? Dark winter mornings. Particularly prominent were complaints from parents, who didn’t like their children walking to school in the dark.

A 1975 study by the US Department of Transportation concluded that a year-round switch possibly isn’t a great idea, proposing instead a schedule change. “We conclude that modest overall benefits might be realized by a shift from the historic 6-month DST system (May through October) to an 8-month DST system (March through October),” the paper concludes. This, notably, is pretty much what the US has been doing since 2007.

The past isn’t a prediction of the future—it’s possible switching to year-round daylight savings would go differently today. Walking to school is less common, for one thing, and streets are better lit. All the same, it’s worth realizing this has been tried before.

#4591. GM to Pay $220 Million in Settlement After Alleged Privacy Violations

General Motors was reportedly selling millions of drivers’ data to insurance companies. Now, the company will fork over millions to 35 states and the District of Columbia.

General Motors is set to pay $220 million in a settlement with the attorneys general of 35 states and the District of Columbia after claims that the automaker sold drivers’ location and behavior data to brokers without permission.

GM’s Smart Driver program sits at the heart of the settlement. The driver monitoring system was meant to log driving data to help monitor driving habits, and was active between 2016 and 2024. However, the program regularly logged hard braking and speeding events, which GM then sold to data brokers under contracts that were used for insurance products, the group of attorneys general claims.

“The coalition’s investigation found that in reality, GM sold this information to data brokers under contracts that specified the data was to be used for insurance products. The data brokers sold the data to insurance companies, who could then change the drivers’ premiums based on their driving habits. GM did not disclose to drivers that their data would be sold for this purpose,” a statement from New York attorney general Letitia James reads.

“Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” a GM spokesperson said to Reuters.

Over 370,000 drivers enrolled in Smart Driver weren’t even aware that the program was tracking their driving, the attorneys general claim. The OnStar app apparently said that they were not enrolled in Smart Driver before GM quietly un-enrolled them without notification. One driver even reportedly faced a 22 percent increase in insurance premiums because of “personal driving information provided by a data broker.”

Many customers signed up for Smart Driver at dealerships when purchasing a new vehicle; GM offered OnStar and Smart Driver as a one-step package deal to customers buying new vehicles, with heavy incentives for dealerships to increase sign-up rates. New York AG James claims that GM offered bonuses based in part on how many customers they signed up for GM’s connected vehicle services, including Smart Driver, and even ranked dealerships based on their enrollment numbers.

“People bought a car, not a tracking device,” as Oregon attorney general Dan Rayfield put it in a statement.

Settlement money will be doled out to consumers in Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Hawai’i, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Kentucky, Maine, Massachusetts, Maryland, Michigan, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia. GM previously paid $12.75 million to settle a California investigation into an alleged sale of drive data to brokers.

#4590. What to do if you hit a deer

Published Oct 31, 2026 2:07 PM EDT

When you think of the fall season, chances are that gorgeous foliage, brisk sweater weather, and Halloween decorations come to mind. Deer, on the other hand, think of sex.

Deer breeding behavior, known as the rut, aligns with the changing length of daylight. As daylight decreases, buck (male deer) and doe (female deer) hormones increase. While in southern states the rut can last several months, it only runs for a short period of time during the fall in the Northeast.

During the rut, bucks seek out does that are ready to breed, and the amorous pursuit can be intense. Because some bucks are so obsessed with breeding, they can eat little and burn through up to 20 percent of their body weight during the season. And just like love-crazed high schoolers, deer during the rut are more distracted and less cautious, as well as more active during the day than they usually are.

“During this period, many yearling bucks leave their birth areas in search of new territory, sometimes dozens of miles away. At the same time, adult bucks are actively roaming their home ranges in pursuit of doe, often chasing those they encounter,” according to Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in Pennsylvania.

What’s more, “The end of daylight-saving time means more vehicles will be on the road during dusk and dawn, which are the peak hours for deer movement.”

In fact, most deer-vehicle accidents take place in October through December. While there are things you can do to lessen your chances of hitting one—such as staying alert and paying close attention when you see deer crossing signs—sometimes accidents are unavoidable. So what should you do if you hit a deer?

Safely pull over and turn your emergency flashers on. While your instinct might be to go see the deer or move the body off of the road, resist the temptation. Care for any injured passengers, and call 911. The dispatchers will send the appropriate authorities to help.

And if you narrowly avoided one deer, remember that, “deer often travel in groups and walk single file,” per the Raven Ridge Wildlife Center. “So even if one deer successfully crosses the road in front of a driver, it doesn’t mean the threat is over. Another could be right behind it.”

#4589. An Uncompromising Fraternal Twin: We Drive the All-Electric 2027 BMW i3

It may not look all that different, but the electric i3 sedan differs from its 3-series siblings in a few key ways.

While BMW’s latest i3 may look like a carbon copy of its gas-powered 3-series sibling, using the gasser to underpin the EV would incur all manner of compromise. BMW did this with its i4 and the 430i models, and the concessions are obvious. In order to get a battery-electric powertrain tucked in the 430i’s body, BMW had to limit the battery size while using air springs to manage the car’s newfound mass. BMW wasn’t willing to make those sacrifices for its electric 3, and as a result, the i3 is actually quite different from its internal-combustion sibling.

The Munich-built BMW i3 50 xDrive sedan shares nothing with the new Dingolfing-made M350 and 330 models, except the front grille, the mirror housings, and possibly the door handles. Everything else is different, and that is reflected by a 1.5-inch stretch in wheelbase, plus some extra height and width. The length, on the other hand, differs only by a few hairs. But the difference is so much more than numbers on a page. Without having to worry about fitting an inline-six under the hood, the i3’s cabin is pushed forward, and the windshield glass picks up some extra rake. The Neue Klasse styling applied to both cars is effective at hiding these differences, but keen eyes may still pick up on the slightly steeper hood and the shorter front-wheel-to-door-edge gap.

See all results for new 2027 BMW i3 for sale near 20147

Adjusting the wheelbase and vehicle height was necessary to fit the electric drivetrain BMW wanted in there, and as a result, we think the i3 50 xDrive outshines the i4. The prime mover is a current-excited synchronous rear motor making 322 horsepower and 321 pound-feet of torque, the same kind of e-motor in the i4. However, the i3’s front motor has been changed to a 165-hp, 188-lb-ft induction motor, and that alteration makes it more efficient because there is less drag when it isn’t engaged. It’s more efficient at speed too. Accounting for the usual fuzzy EV-motor math, the i3 50’s full output is a meaty 463 horses and 476 pound-feet, enough to push the electric 3 to 60 mph in an estimated 4.2 seconds.

Also unlike the i4, the i3’s battery is not a limit in any way, shape, or form. It’s much more capacious, toting 112 kWh instead of the i4’s 84 kWh. We estimate the range at a fantastic 450 miles (the EPA has yet to rate it), which is a bit higher than BMW’s own number, since the electric iX3 SUV’s official range also surpassed BMW’s initial internal figure. The two vehicles share a powertrain, so we figure the powertrain’s overachieving nature will transfer from SUV to sedan too. On the charging front, the pack’s 800-volt architecture means it can gulp down electricity at 400 kilowatts (if you can find a charger that can support it). A NACS port is standard equipment, with an included adapter for SAE Combo charging.

See all results for new 2027 BMW i3 for sale near 20147

Despite leaving the optional M adaptive dampers at home, the car we drove seemed expertly tuned, with a ride that was taut but never too firm. The battery’s low mass helped keep the car feeling planted in corners, with just enough roll stiffness to keep body lean disciplined without introducing harshness or head toss to upset the proceedings.

And we pushed it hard in corners, too. Some of this feeling comes from BMW’s “Heart of Joy” computer, which sorts out the steering, friction braking, regenerative braking, throttle inputs, and more—in a claimed one-tenth of the time that previous BMW software stacks required. Brake-based rear differential action, something we usually don’t care for, was silky smooth in this system and felt for all the world like an electronically controlled rear diff. Brake response is uncommonly good, and there is enough regenerative braking capacity that nearly all your routine stops will be handled magnetically.

The one thing we were less effervescent about was the steering feel. The i3’s helm is certainly accurate and direct enough, but it doesn’t quite have the feel and feedback of the gas-powered M350 we drove (and reviewed separately). Perhaps that differentiator is there intentionally; after all, there’s a sportier i3 M60 model coming.

At least the i3 we drove didn’t have the dorky steering wheel with odd vertical spokes. (The optional M Sport wheel puts said spokes in a vastly more normal location.) BMW’s trick Panoramic Vision screen works even better in the i3 than it does in the M350, because the dash-spanning display strip is more visible above the wheel, yet it doesn’t hide the road. The taller but more steeply angled hood works in its favor, for sure. The central touchscreen is the same 17.9-inch display found in the M350 and has all the same characteristics. On the positive side, it looks great, and the angled shape is quite natural. On the other hand, let’s just say that vent aiming is better done manually, rather than via touchscreen controls, and there are other functions that could benefit from a real button or two. You can save a few bucks by not opting for the head-up display, which seems redundant when you already have a wealth of information at the base of the windscreen.

We also like the i3’s soaring panoramic glass roof, which provides an abundance of headroom. Rear-seat space is slightly larger than the M350’s, but toe space beneath the front seat can be tighter if the front occupant has their chair lowered to the floor. BMW doesn’t have a U.S.-specific figure for trunk space just yet, but preliminary German figures place its 15 cubic feet just one cube in arrears of the M350 gasser.

The BMW i3 50 xDrive will launch in the first quarter of 2027, right alongside the gas-powered 3-series lineup. It starts at $62,850, which seems like a great deal for all you get. The i3 feels mighty special and has the potential to draw new buyers into the electric fold. It’s got gobs of range, it charges fast, and it delivers speed and poise like a proper BMW.

#4588. VW Suspends ID.Golf EV Development Amid Financial Pressures: Report

The electric Golf is apparently being put on the shelf, at least for now.

It was only a few months ago that Volkswagen was showing teasers of the next-gen electric Golf to folks behind closed doors, but a new report now claims development on said vehicle is suspended until further notice—a development pause that is one of the many cuts being made by the Volkswagen Group as it looks to save cash amid financial pressures.

The hatchback, which was exxpected to be named ID.Golf, was meant to be the electric successor to the ID.3. Reuters reports that it viewed a memo written by CEO Thomas Schaefer that revealed the delay. "I know what the Golf means for Volkswagen and for Wolfsburg. That's why this decision was really not an easy one for us," the internal memo reportedly said. “We simply can't afford this work right now.”

Whether or not Volkswagen would sell the supposed ID.Golf in the U.S. remains a question. We haven’t seen a standard Golf on sale here since the introduction of the current Mk.8 generation; the GTI and Golf R performance variants live on, thankfully, but an electric version sure would open the discussion back up to bringing the mainstream version to American shores again.

But the news is a large blow to those in Europe who might’ve been expecting a successor to the ID.3 before the end of the decade. VW recently revealed the ID.3 Neo (above) that brought sweeping changes to the car, at least ensuring there will be an electric, Golf-like car on sale across the Pond for some time. Still, the jump to the ID.Golf is meant to be a large one, as VW planned the new model along with a transition to a new Scalable Systems Platform (SSP) architecture.

The caveat to this news is that VW is expressing this as simply a delay in development. That means the company is still planning on picking things up at a later date, so presumably, an ID.Golf is still in the product roadmap. We just don’t know when it could arrive.

#4587. Putrid blood shoots from these lizards’ eyes

Published Nov 1, 2026 8:03 AM EST

Horned lizards are spiky cuties. Three to six inches long, these lizards are coated with sharp spines all across their hard, sand-colored backs. But in the dry deserts and prairies they call home, they are still vulnerable. As they scuttle through the protective brush in arid landscapes from Mexico to southern Canada, they have to reckon with hungry coyotes, snakes that will gobble them whole, and even peckish roadrunners. That’s why multiple species of horned lizards have developed a weird but effective deterrent: blood.

And not just any blood: These lizards shoot foul-smelling blood out of their eyes, sending many would-be predators scattering. But experts say the lizards are now facing other threats to their survival that even a fountain of eye blood can’t deter.

Dean Williams, a professor of biology at Texas Christian University, studies horned lizard populations in central Texas. He says that blood squirting is really a backup defense for the lizards. “Their first line of defense is going to be crypsis,” aka blending in with their background, says Williams.

Williams and his colleagues tag the lizards they study with radio trackers that pinpoint their location to an area roughly the size of an office desk. Even then, he says, it can take “15 minutes of rummaging” to find the lizard in their scrubland habitat. The lizards don’t move much, he added, blending in with nearby rocks.

But when hiding doesn’t work, the lizards deploy their unusual, foul-smelling blood, which Williams says is a product of an equally foul delicacy. “Their diet consists mainly of these large Pogonomyrmex or harvester ants,” says Williams. Harvester ants defend themselves using neurotoxic venom that causes intense, long-lasting, stinging pain in mammals.

Unfortunately for the harvester ants, this toxin doesn’t even slightly deter horned lizards, who eat the ants in large numbers. A 2024 study identified that a compound in the lizards’ blood spiked after scientists fed them harvester ants. The researchers think this compound, possibly adapted from ant venom, makes the lizards’ blood taste foul.

However, that gross metabolized ant blood coursing through the lizards’ veins wouldn’t be much help if it only annoyed a predator after it had already bitten off the lizard’s head. That’s where the lizards’ unusual squirting mechanism comes in handy.

Williams explains that the lizards can build up pressure in blood vessels around their sinuses. Eventually, the vessels burst, shooting the toxic blood out in jets. Mammals exposed to the stream of blood react with notable disgust. There seems to be little consequence for the lizards, even though in one experiment, a lizard lost 6.8 percent of its body mass after squirting blood when exposed to a dog.

The foul-smelling blood doesn’t protect the lizards from every predator, though. Roadrunners and other birds of prey still chow down on them, says Williams. To guard against birds, the lizards use the sharp horns on the back of their heads to stab at predators that try to seize them in their beaks.

The lizards’ foul blood also does little to deter snakes. Instead, the lizards have evolved specialized strategies to evade these predators. Rattlesnakes are lazy hunters that wait in the shadows for prey to approach. Horned lizards have learned to run away from these snakes.

But Williams says they use a different strategy if hunted by a coachwhip or racer snake. These fearsome snakes can easily chase down the lizards, who instead quickly flatten their bodies against the dirt, showing the snake their spiked backs, which makes them harder to swallow.

But despite these bespoke, often ingenious defense mechanisms, horned lizards in the Lone Star State are under serious threat. They’ve disappeared from their habitat across eastern Texas. Williams says that industrialization is devastating lizard populations. “They seem to be very sensitive to those habitat changes,” he says.

In small towns, the lizards can live alongside humans when their natural brush habitat is preserved. But in towns where humans cleared the brush, “the lizards just disappeared,” Williams says.

Horned lizards are ectotherms, meaning they must change their behavior to keep their body temperature under control. In the blistering heat of a Texas summer, the lizards simply can’t keep their bodies within safe limits once the cool shade of vegetation has disappeared.

Harvester ants provide horned lizards with one of their strongest defenses. But another ant species has become the second major challenge to the lizards’ survival. Fire ants are an invasive species in the United States. They swarm the nests of ground-dwelling lizards, eating vulnerable eggs, or even attacking and killing young lizards.

That’s where conservation efforts, like the one Williams works on with zoos across Texas, play an important role. The program releases nearly a thousand young lizards each year.

These hatchlings, which can easily fit in the palm of a hand, are packaged in individual Tupperware containers and then released in the desert scrub. Williams says that his graduate student, Kira Gangbin, has been working on a targeted poison to cut down fire ant numbers and help keep these hatchlings alive. These efforts will hopefully keep horned lizard populations thriving for many more years. Just remember: If you come across a horned lizard on a hike through the Texas desert, give it a wide berth, or risk a foul, bloody surprise.

#4585. Jasion Poki review: The Electric Minibike that packs heavy-duty fun

In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the Jasion Poki.

The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.

So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.

This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.

That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.

OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.

Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.

I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.

Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.

Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

The Poki is currently priced at $1,799, and customers can get 5% off with the code Electrek.

#4584. Fierce turtles square off in a rare woodland turf battle

Published Nov 1, 2026 10:10 AM EST

At first, it appears that two turtles with yellow spots are calmly sitting side by side. Suddenly, one of them turns, slowly—and lunges out with its head, its open beak clearly trying to take an aggressive chomp out of its neighbor. Moments later, the turtle tries again. Now, both reptiles are going head-to-head, though each is retracted into the protection of its shell.

The two combatants are male eastern box turtles (Terrapene carolina carolina) competing for dominance. Eastern box turtles are a subspecies of the common box turtle (Terrapene carolina), with bright orange and yellow coloring on its dark shell. They live throughout the eastern and midwestern United States.

“I wouldn’t say that they’re normally aggressive, but male box turtles can definitely become territorial, especially since males’ home ranges (the area they frequently occupy) often overlap,” Eamon Caffrey, the turtle research coordinator at Mass Audubon who captured the video, tells Popular Science. “We do occasionally see this sort of brawling behavior between two males when out in the field; you just have to get lucky enough to actually witness it. This experience was a first for me, and I was thrilled to capture it on camera.”

Over the summer, another Mass Audubon staff member saw two male box turtles opting for a pushing contest instead of biting. At one point, one of the two flipped the other contestant onto its back and pushed him down a small hill. Box turtle battles can also feature spinning each other around.

“From my understanding, fights between male box turtles are much more opportunistic than anything else,” Caffrey tells Popular Science. “Often, when two males come in contact, they will display a variety of aggressive behaviors that can include head butting, shell ramming, biting, pushing, and shoving – all in attempts to assert dominance. These disputes are often territorial but can be over mates as well.”

What’s more, the turtle with the darker shell is a well-known individual over 30 years old. Caffrey says he’s seen him various times this year, and since capturing the video the celebrity reptile has been spending time in an area where the Mass Audubon team frequently spot two to three adult females. However, there’s been no trace of his opponent.

“Does that mean he ‘won’ the battle?” Caffrey muses. “Who knows.”

#4583. 20 Best Chronographs for Drivers

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

These chronographs bring together mechanical ingenuity, motorsport heritage, and distinctive design, in a range of price points.

This article was updated in October 2026.

Few watch complications have as much character as the chronograph. Originally developed as a tool for measuring elapsed time, chronos became an essential piece of equipment in aviation, motorsport, and professional timing.

Today, the chronograph remains one of watchmaking’s most recognizable designs, with twin pushers, layered subdials, and tachymeter scales giving even a simple wristwatch a distinctly technical look. It’s also one of the few complications where the mechanical function is just as satisfying to operate as it is to look at.

For anyone getting into watches, chronographs offer an especially interesting entry point. The category spans everything from affordable Japanese quartz movements to sophisticated Swiss automatics, with plenty of variation in case architecture, dial layout, and movement design along the way.

There’s a lot to learn too, such as the difference between a standard chronograph and a flyback, the appeal of a column-wheel movement, or why certain vintage racing references have become so collectible. You can spend a little or a lot and still come away with a watch that has a story behind it.

We put together this selection with both new buyers and seasoned enthusiasts in mind. Some are modern interpretations of historically important designs, others have direct ties to motorsport, and a few offer interesting movements or complications that make them stand out from the usual three-hand watch.

💡 Expert Tip: Mechanical chronographs have more moving parts than standard watches, making routine servicing especially important. Plan on a professional service every five to seven years, and avoid operating the pushers underwater unless the watch is specifically designed for it.

The Omega Speedmaster features a stainless-steel case and bracelet with a fixed bezel and black aluminum ring displaying tachymeter markings. The 40mm round case houses a gray analog dial with luminescent silver-tone hands, index hour markers, and numeral minute markers at 5-minute intervals. The timepiece offers a date display and three chronograph subdials for 60 seconds, 30 minutes, and 12 hours. Powered by an Omega calibre 3330 automatic movement with a 52-hour power reserve, it has a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal and a pull/push crown.

The Seiko SSB479P1 features a 38.7mm stainless-steel case and bracelet and a Hardlex crystal. Its dial features luminous hands and index hour markers, a small seconds subdial, a 24-hour indicator, and a date display. Powered by Seiko’s 8T63 quartz movement, the chronograph measures elapsed time up to 60 minutes in one-fifth-second increments. A fixed tachymeter scale provides a way to calculate average speed, while 50-meter water resistance makes the watch suitable for everyday use.

Seiko has long been a gateway brand for watch enthusiasts, and this model offers a relatively affordable way to get a well-executed Japanese chronograph. Its sub-40mm case is also a welcome change from the oversize sports watches that have dominated much of the category.

The Fossil Signature CS-1 Master Calendar Chronoquartz features a 42mm stainless-steel case with a domed sapphire crystal and a dial designed to combine chronograph timing with calendar functions. Its layout includes day and month apertures, a central date hand that tracks the date around the outer chapter ring, and recessed subdials for the chronograph. Power comes from the Swiss Ronda 5040.F quartz movement, which drives the chronograph and triple-calendar display. The watch is available with a stainless-steel bracelet or an Italian leather strap, depending on the reference, and offers 50-meter water resistance. Its record-inspired dial texture and carefully arranged displays give it a more technical look than a conventional dress chronograph.

For someone just getting into watches, the combination of chronograph and full calendar complications offers plenty to explore, while its unconventional layout gives it a little more personality than a typical entry-level fashion watch.

The Hamilton American Classic Intra-Matic Chronograph features a 40mm stainless-steel case with a vintage-inspired profile and a contrasting two-register dial. Luminous hands and markers provide visibility, while a tachymeter scale adds a motorsport-inspired touch. The automatic version is powered by Hamilton’s H-31 movement, with a 60-hour power reserve, while the hand-wound Intra-Matic Chronograph H uses the H-51 caliber with the same power reserve. Both feature a sapphire crystal with antireflective coating and 100-meter water resistance.

Hamilton’s connection to American watchmaking and the Intra-Matic’s clear inspiration from its historic chronographs give this model some real substance for vintage-watch fans. The hand-wound version is particularly appealing.

The Tissot PRX Chronograph Automatic features a 42mm stainless-steel case with the collection’s signature angular profile and an integrated steel bracelet. Its dial uses a contrasting three-register layout, with chronograph counters at three, six, and nine o’clock, and a date display. Powered by Tissot’s automatic Valjoux A05.H31 movement, the watch offers a 60-hour power reserve. A scratch-resistant sapphire crystal protects the dial, and the case is water-resistant to 100 meters.

The PRX has become one of the more recognizable modern Swiss sports-watch designs, and the chronograph adds a layer of mechanical interest to its integrated-bracelet format. For someone building a collection, it offers a taste of the Seventies sports-watch aesthetic without the price tag attached to many of its luxury counterparts.

The Timex Q Continental Chronograph features a 36mm stainless-steel case with brushed surfaces, polished edges, and an integrated stainless-steel bracelet. Its textured dial features contrasting chronograph subdials, luminous hands and hour markers, and a fixed tachymeter bezel for calculating average speed. Powered by a quartz chronograph movement, it includes a stopwatch function and 24-hour display. A mineral crystal protects the dial, while 50-meter water resistance makes it suitable for everyday wear.

Its compact proportions and distinctly retro styling make it an appealing entry point for collectors interested in the smaller, more experimental sports watches of the Seventies and Eighties.

The Bulova 150th Anniversary Shelby Racer Chronograph features a 43mm stainless-steel bullhead case inspired by the 1967 Shelby Ford Mustang GT500. Its blue and white color scheme carries across the dial and rubber strap, while a black tachymeter ring, 12 o’clock crown and pushers, and Shelby Cobra branding reinforce its racing theme. Powered by Bulova’s Precisionist quartz movement, the chronograph can measure elapsed time to one-thousandth of a second. An antireflective sapphire crystal protects the dial, and the watch is water-resistant to 50 meters. The limited edition was produced in a run of 7500 pieces and originally included a miniature GT500 model. Its unusual bullhead layout and direct connection to American muscle-car history make it an interesting crossover piece for collectors who enjoy watches as much for their automotive associations as their movements.

The Junghans Form C Chronoscope features a 40mm stainless-steel case measuring 10.5mm thick, with a clean, minimalist dial and a slim profile. Its matte-finished dial features luminous hands, a small seconds subdial, a date display, and two chronograph counters for measuring elapsed minutes and hours. Powered by a quartz movement, the watch offers straightforward timekeeping without the maintenance demands of a mechanical chronograph. A scratch-resistant sapphire crystal protects the dial, while 50-meter water resistance makes it suitable for everyday use.

Junghans has a long association with German design, particularly the restrained Bauhaus-influenced aesthetic, and the Form C is a good example of that philosophy. It makes a compelling choice for someone who appreciates thoughtful industrial design and prefers a chronograph that doesn’t rely on oversize cases or racing-inspired graphics.

This Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar Chronograph is considered a “Grand Complication,” the absolute peak of watchmaking produced by Patek, one of watchmaking’s most prestigious and important manufacturers. This watch features a rose-gold case, but the real draw here is the movement. The self-winding caliber CHR 29-535 PS Q movement is visible through a sapphire-crystal caseback, and on the dial side of the watch, you’ll spot rattrapante chronograph hands displayed alongside perpetual calendar and moon-phase displays. The 5205 is truly a masterpiece of high horology, combining ultimate functionality with elegant design and surpassing craftsmanship. Note: This is a pre-owned watch.

The Portugieser is a classic chrono with a clean, elegant design. It has a round stainless-steel case, measuring 41mm in diameter and 13mm in thickness. The dial features two subdials at the six and 12 o’clock positions. It runs on IWC-manufactured caliber 69355 automatic movement with a power reserve of approximately 46 hours, visible through a sapphire-crystal caseback. The watch comes with either a leather or stainless-steel strap, is water-resistant up to 30 meters, and is a popular choice among watch enthusiasts and collectors. Note: This is a pre-owned watch.

The Tissot PRS 516 features a stainless-steel case with a sporty dial, luminous hands and hour markers, and a fixed tachymeter bezel. The automatic version uses Tissot’s own A05.H31 movement, with a power reserve of approximately 60 hours. Its chronograph function includes a central seconds hand and a 30-minute counter, alongside a date display. A scratch-resistant sapphire-crystal and transparent caseback showcase the watch’s construction.

The collection’s roots in motorsport-inspired design date back to the Sixties, giving it a bit of history beyond the usual modern sports-watch formula. The automatic version is especially appealing to collectors who want a traditional Swiss mechanical chronograph with a more overt racing influence.

The limited-edition Chopard Mille Miglia GT XL embodies the excitement of the historic Mille Miglia race. It features a sturdy stainless-steel case, automatic chronograph movement, and a white dial with easy-to-read numerals and indices. The watch’s functions include hour, minute, and seconds hands, a date window with a magnification loupe, and subdials that track the elapsed minutes and hours of the chronograph, plus a continuously running seconds hand. This Swiss-made watch features a 48-hour power reserve and a 44mm case diameter. This watch is limited to just 1000 pieces.

The Prospex Speedtimer is a solar-powered, precision timepiece inspired by the classic chronograph designs of the Sixties. Featuring a Seiko V192 movement with a six-month power reserve, it boasts a black dial, a tachymeter bezel, LumiBrite hands and markers, a curved sapphire crystal, a date calendar, stainless-steel construction, and 100-meter water resistance.

The Navitimer was initially designed for aviation professionals and enthusiasts, a portmanteau of “navigation” and “time.” This take on the classic Navitimer features a slide-rule bezel to complete basic calculations, a self-winding automatic movement, and a chronograph function, plus three subdials. It comes in a stainless-steel or 18k-gold case, with luminous markers and a date-display window on the dial. The watch is water-resistant to 30 meters and has a power reserve of up to 70 hours, making it a reliable and functional watch for everyday wear. Note: This is a pre-owned watch.

The TAG Heuer Formula 1 Chronograph features a 43mm stainless-steel case with a fixed tachymeter bezel and a sporty blue dial with luminous hands and applied hour markers. Its quartz chronograph movement measures elapsed time in tenths of a second and includes a 30-minute counter and date display. A scratch-resistant sapphire crystal protects the dial, while the screw-down crown and 200-meter water resistance give the watch added durability. Depending on the reference, the bezel may use ceramic or coated steel, and the watch is available with different dial and bracelet configurations.

TAG Heuer’s motorsport history makes the Formula 1 line a natural fit for automotive enthusiasts, and its connection to the brand’s racing partnerships gives it an identity beyond its stopwatch functionality. It’s also an approachable way into one of the most recognizable names in Swiss sports watches.

The primary distinction between a regular watch and a chronograph lies in a chronograph’s stopwatch functions. A chronograph enables its users to measure the elapsed time of an event, like one lap of a racetrack or how long you’ve had your steaks on the grill. All the while, your watch is keeping track of the current time.

In addition to basic timekeeping and stopwatch capabilities, many chronograph watches come equipped with a tachymeter, a scale used to measure speed based on elapsed time over a specific distance (usually one mile), and a telemeter, which measures distance based on the speed of sound and elapsed time. Water resistance is another common feature, protecting the watch from damage due to moisture or immersion in water.

Chronographs come in various types, each with its own characteristics:

A chronograph combines the functionality of a traditional watch with a built-in stopwatch. This allows users to measure elapsed time and split times, which makes it ideal for driving.

To use the stopwatch functions on a chronograph timepiece, you press the corresponding pushers (button) on the side of the watch to start, stop, and reset the stopwatch. Certain chronograph watches may have additional pushers for more advanced functions like split or lap times. Due to the extra mechanical complexity required, watches with more pushers will typically cost more than monopusher (single-pusher) timepieces.

A tachymeter is a scale on the bezel or dial of certain chronograph watches. Its purpose is to measure the speed of an object using the watch’s built-in stopwatch, based on the time passed. To use the tachymeter, start the chronograph function when something starts (like a car crossing a start line) and stop it when it’s finished (when the car hits the finish line). The tachymeter scale will then display the car’s average speed, based on the time it took to get from A to B.

Proper maintenance of your chronograph depends on its type. Mechanical chronograph watches require regular servicing (roughly every 5–7 years) to ensure optimal performance. Quartz chronograph watches may need battery replacements, and solar-powered watches should be exposed to light regularly to maintain their charge. Be sure to always follow the manufacturer’s maintenance guidelines.
